blocks.x: COM SKILLS 157 · Communication Skills · Topic 3

Punctuation is what turns a string of words into a sentence a reader can actually follow — it tells the eye where to pause, where a thought ends, where a list begins, and where a speaker's exact words start and stop. This topic works through every major mark of punctuation in English, its correct uses, and the common misuses to avoid in academic and business writing.

By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Define punctuation and explain why capitalization, although it also aids clarity, is not itself classed as a punctuation mark.
2Use the three end marks correctly — the period/full stop, the question mark, and the exclamation mark — including their less obvious uses (initials, decimals, abbreviations, doubtful facts).

3Apply the comma's ten main uses (series, dates, numbers, adverbials, quotations, clauses, salutations, adjectives, interjections, appositives, introductory phrases) and recognise the situations where a comma should not be used.

4Distinguish the colon from the semicolon, use each to join or introduce material correctly, and avoid the classic misuses of both (colon after a preposition/verb, semicolon as a mark of introduction).
5Use the hyphen, dash, and apostrophe correctly, including the detailed rules for dividing a word at the end of a line, and form contractions, plurals, and possessives without error.
6Apply quotation marks, underlining, the ellipsis, and the rules of capitalization to titles, direct quotations, omitted text, and proper nouns.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Punctuation Non-alphabetical symbols used in writing for the purposes of clarity and comprehension. Punctuation marks tell the reader where a sentence pauses, stops, asks a question, lists items, or quotes someone else's exact words.

Capitalization is not punctuation Not every symbol used to aid clarity in writing is a punctuation mark. Capitalization — writing the first letter of a word as an uppercase letter — is a separate convention of written English. It is covered in this topic because it works alongside punctuation to signal meaning (e.g. proper nouns, the start of a sentence), but it is not itself classified as punctuation.

The thirteen marks of punctuation
Period (full stop) . · Question mark ? · Exclamation mark ! · Dash –– · Hyphen - · Apostrophe ' · Underlining · Comma , · Semicolon ; · Colon : · Quotation marks “” · Parentheses () · Brackets []
End Marks→ Comma→ Colon & Semicolon→ Hyphen, Dash & Apostrophe→ Quotation Marks & Capitalization
Where every sentence stops — and pauses

Every sentence in English must close with one of three end marks, and inside the sentence the comma does more work than any other mark of punctuation — which is exactly why it is also the most frequently misused.
What is an end mark?
End mark A punctuation mark that comes at the end of a sentence. It lets the reader know when to stop. There are three end marks: the period (full stop), the question mark, and the exclamation mark.
Period (full stop) .

items: 1At the end of a (declarative) sentence: I love my country.
2After an initial: Akosua B. Antwi
3As a decimal point: $2.50
4After an abbreviation: Mrs.

blocks.x: Question mark ?

items: 1After a direct question: Do you know the motto of KNUST?
2To show doubt about a fact, placed in parentheses: The Gold Coast was renamed Ghana on a Thursday (?)

blocks.x: Exclamation mark !

items: 1To express strong feeling: What a shock!
2After some imperative sentences: Come here!

blocks.x: Caution: never stack exclamation marks Never use multiple exclamation marks in school writing assignments or in business letters. Wrong: I need my money now!!! One exclamation mark is always enough.
The comma — ten essential uses

items: 1Between items in a series: I know someone who likes orange, pineapple, and banana.
2In dates and addresses: June 24, 2010
3To keep numbers clear: 1,000,000
4To set off adverbials at the start of a sentence: Yesterday, we visited the library.
5To set off a direct quotation: The Hen replied, “My axe is sick.”
6Sometimes between two (independent) clauses: Aquarium workers love animals, so they rescue hurt ones.
7After salutations in personal letters: Dear Uncle Jim,
8To separate adjectives of equal rank: I like the feel of cold, salty water when I go wading.
9To set off interjections: Wow, look at that sunrise!
10To set off appositives: My father, a great cook, makes the best fried rice in town.

blocks.x: Introductory phrases and clauses A comma also sets off an introductory phrase or clause from the main sentence: After checking my knee pads, I started off.
Unnecessary commas — do not use a comma…
To separate subject from predicate
Wrong: We, requested that the road be resurfaced. The subject “We” must never be cut off from its verb by a comma.
Before an indirect quotation
Wrong: The candidate stated that, he was against taxation. No comma is needed before reported (indirect) speech introduced by “that.”
Between two independent clauses (comma splice)
Wrong: The foreman told me to be there early, I told him I couldn't. Two complete sentences joined only by a comma is a comma splice — a stronger mark (period or semicolon) is needed.
Indiscriminately to replace an omitted word
Wrong: Frank said, he would come to see me. The comma is incorrectly standing in for the omitted word “that” (“Frank said that he would come to see me.”)

blocks.title: Golden rule: when in doubt, leave it out

items: Never insert a comma in any situation unless it adds to clarity and understanding.
Overloaded example to avoid: Naturally, the first thing you should do, after reporting for work, is to see your supervisor.
Overloaded example to avoid: After the play, Martha and I went home, by taxicab, because we wanted, at all cost, to avoid subway crowds. — most of these commas add clutter rather than clarity.

blocks.x: Signalling what comes next — and joining equals

The colon points forward — it tells the reader to "watch for what's coming." The semicolon points sideways — it joins two independent, equally weighted statements with a pause stronger than a comma but short of a full stop.
The colon

Colon The colon is a mark of expectation or addition. Its primary function is to signal the reader to “watch for what's coming.” It commonly introduces a list, and can also introduce a single word, phrase, or clause.

items: 1To introduce a word, phrase, or clause, or after an introductory statement: This is my problem: what do I do now?

2To separate introductory words from a long or formal quotation which follows: Jefferson concluded his First Inaugural Address as follows: “And may that Infinite Power which rules the destinies of the universe…”
3To introduce a list: the classic use — a full statement followed by a colon, followed by the items in the list.

blocks.x: Other places the colon appears

c: Chapters and verses of the Bible

blocks.x: Do not overuse the colon
Between a preposition and its object
Wrong: I am fond of: New Orleans, Seattle, Denver. The colon should not split “of” from the places it governs.
Between a verb and its object
Wrong: He liked to see: TV plays, movies, and sitcoms. Also wrong: She likes a number of activities, such as: swimming, dancing, and cooking.
The semicolon

Semicolon The semicolon is a stronger mark of punctuation than the comma; it signifies a greater break or longer pause between sentence elements. Remember: the semicolon is used only between elements of equal rank — it is entirely a mark of coordination.

items: 1To separate independent clauses not joined by a simple conjunction: “If you make people think they're thinking, they'll love you; if you really make them think, they'll hate you.” — Marquis

2To separate independent clauses joined by a conjunctive adverb (also, anyhow, besides, consequently, furthermore, however, moreover, otherwise, therefore, thus, etc.): This job is not simple; however, it's exciting and rewarding.

3Between independent clauses which are lengthy or contain internal punctuation: “As long as war is regarded as wicked, it will have its fascination; when it is looked upon as vulgar, it will cease to be popular.” — Wilde

blocks.x: Do not overuse the semicolon

The “no period, no semicolon” test Ordinarily, the semicolon has the same function as a period: it indicates a complete break, the end of one thought and the beginning of another. One fairly safe guide is: no period, no semicolon. Wrong: Inasmuch as Joe has a fiery temper; we have to be careful what we say to him. (a comma should be used instead, since the first part is not an independent clause).
Not as a mark of introduction
Wrong: Dear Sir; — a colon, not a semicolon, follows a formal salutation.
Not as a summarizing mark
Wrong: Answering the phone, typing, filing; these were my duties last summer. A dash, not a semicolon, correctly introduces the summarizing clause.

items: Colon: forward-pointing — introduces a list, word, phrase, clause, or long quotation; also used in special formatting situations (time, titles, references).
Semicolon: sideways-joining — links two independent clauses of equal rank, with or without a conjunctive adverb, especially when they are lengthy or already contain commas.
Both are "stronger than a comma" but neither replaces a full stop when the two parts are entirely separate thoughts.

blocks.x: Joining, breaking, and shortening words

These three short marks do very different jobs: the hyphen joins parts of a word (or splits one across a line break), the dash marks a sudden break or shift in thought, and the apostrophe shows omission or possession.
The hyphen -
Hyphen A mark of separation used between parts of a word.

items: 1To separate (join) the parts of compound words: fast-moving; sister-in-law; half-asleep; X-ray; know-it-all; forty-seven; three-fourths
2To indicate the division of a word broken at the end of a line when you run out of room — divide only at syllable breaks: knowl-edge, ste-nog-ra-pher
3Between numbers in fractions: three-fourths

blocks.x: Rules for dividing a word at the end of a line
Never divide
A monosyllable (one-syllable word) — e.g. strength, laughed — or a contraction.
Never divide
On a syllable with a silent vowel — e.g. climbed, yelled.
Never divide
A word of only four letters — e.g. also, only, open.
Do divide
Two consonants standing between vowels — e.g. struc-ture, alter-native, exis-ten-tialism.

items: 1Do not divide sums of money.
2Do not divide initials in a name or in proper names.
3Do not divide units of time.

blocks.x: The dash ––

Dash A mark of punctuation used to denote a sudden break or shift in thought — “the interruption, the mark of abruptness, the sob, the stammer, the mark of ignorance.” It is the only mark of punctuation not on the standard keyboard: to type a dash, use two hyphens, with no space preceding or following them.

items: 1To indicate a break or shift in thought: Do we—can we—dare we ask for more money?
2To introduce a word or group of words you wish to emphasize: What he needed most he never got—love.
3To set off strongly distinguished parenthetical material: I think—no, I am positive—that you should go.
4To indicate omission of letters and words: Senator S– was from my hometown. June—October 1990

blocks.x: The apostrophe '

items: 1In contractions: can't
2To form plurals of letters: A's
3In place of omitted numbers or letters: class of '91
4To form singular possessives: sister's
5To form plural possessives: girls'
6To form shared possessives: Jim, Jeb, and Jerry's fish (one fish shared by all three — only the last name takes the apostrophe).

blocks.title: Worked check: choosing the right contraction

items: My unusual parrot ___ eat a single cracker. — the choices are won't, wasn't, isn't, don't. Only won't (will + not) correctly pairs with the base verb form “eat” to express the parrot's ongoing refusal; the others either clash in tense (wasn't/isn't describe a state, not an action) or in subject-verb agreement (don't is used with plural or “I/you” subjects, not a singular parrot).
Every contraction is an apostrophe standing in for omitted letters: won't = will + not (with a spelling change), don't = do + not, isn't = is + not, wasn't = was + not.

blocks.x: Titles, exact words, omissions, and capital letters

This closing section covers how to mark titles (underlining vs. quotation marks), how to punctuate a direct quotation correctly, how to signal omitted text with the ellipsis, and the full set of capitalization rules that work alongside punctuation.
Underlining

Underlining Used for the titles of plays, books, newspapers, magazines, television programs, movies, and CDs — complete, stand-alone works. Examples: The Wiz (play), Exploring an Ocean Tide Pool (book), Pinky and the Brain (television program), The Prince of Egypt (movie).
Quotation marks “”

items: 1To set off a direct quotation — the speaker's exact words: The Hen replied, “My axe is sick.”
2Placement of other punctuation: put commas and periods inside the closing quotation mark.
3To punctuate titles of shorter works — songs, poems, short stories, essays, and chapters of books, and articles in newspapers, magazines, encyclopedias, or electronic sources.

blocks.x: Song
“America the Beautiful”
Short story
“McBroom Tells the Truth”
Chapter
“Water, Water Everywhere”
The ellipsis …

Ellipsis Three spaced periods used to indicate an omission from a quoted passage: Osagyefo Dr. Kwame Nkrumah said: “Our independence is meaningless…” The ellipsis can also mean “and so on,” showing a list continues beyond what is written: There are 16 regions in Ghana: Oti, Ashanti, Bono, Central, Northern…
Capitalization
Proper nouns and proper adjectives Capitalize names of people, and words used as names — such as Mother, Father, Aunt, or Uncle, when they stand in for a person's actual name.
Used as a name
Ask Mother what we're having for lunch. Here “Mother” is being used as her name, so it is capitalized.
Used descriptively
Ask my mother what we're having for lunch. Here “mother” simply describes the relationship, preceded by “my,” so it stays lowercase.

items: 1Geographic names: Earth
2Titles used with names: Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.
3Historical events: Boston Tea Party
4Abbreviations: M.D.
5Organizations: Girl Scouts of America
6Titles (of creative works): Beauty and the Beast
7First word in a sentence, always.
8Days and months: June, Saturday (but not seasons).
9Names of religions, nationalities, and languages: Christianity, Chinese, Spanish
10Official (brand/product) names: Smile toothpaste

blocks.title: Worked check: capitalizing a movie title correctly

items: Question: which sentence uses correct capitalization? A) Have you seen “star wars”? B) One of the main characters is Princess leia. C) My favorite character is Yoda. D) I would like to have a ship like the millennium falcon.
Answer: C. “Yoda” is a proper noun (a character's name) and is correctly capitalized with nothing else in the sentence needing a capital.

A is wrong because the title Star Wars needs both words capitalized. B is wrong because “Leia” is part of the proper name “Princess Leia” and must be capitalized. D is wrong because “Millennium Falcon” is the proper name of a specific ship and both words must be capitalized.
